detail.longDescription:
this endless rain has given me a chance to get into Žores Aleksandrovič Medvedev's giant book "soviet agriculture" from 1987 (full text available here: https://annas-archive.gl/md5/974e404a3542a2e769fa371313c72b60?&check=1 )

i'm about halfway through. i've gotten through the civil war, NEP, the nightmares of collectivization, the famine of the early 30s, WWII, the famine of 1946-47, and am finally into the post-stalin era.

it's so big and so messed up that i don't even know how to approach it in a 2 page spread that should be roughly 50% pictures, and will also include some stories from my mom about her times working on the kolkhoz as a seasonal urban worker.

so this is my basic understanding:

the people who made the revolution were city people and they didn't understand agriculture or the people who lived and worked the fields. they saw agriculture, the peasants, and the land as something to be extracted from for the purpose of building up industry in cities.

those leaders were also totally happy to conduct massive experiments with human lives. nothing was small scale/pilot project/test and see/take a cautious approach. everything was big and URGENT. harvests were failing and people needed to be fed, so they sort of shuddered from one massive reform to another.

it was all made worse because these people really did not value individuals, especially not peasants. in their eyes, the job of the peasants was to stay put and work the fields and give everything to the state and be happy with any scraps that were left over for them.

stalin ruled for 3 decades. he was a murderous tyrant who killed or exiled anyone whose perspectives differed from his own. so anyone with any kind of expertise and integrity who might have been like "this plan is terrible", they were eliminated. this also applied to agricultural scientists and specialists.

he especially had it in for the "kulaks", who were slightly wealthier peasants (REALLY slightly...like 3 cows vs 1 cow per household). hundreds of thousands of them were shipped off to siberia. he also embarked on a completely disastrous collectivization plan in which they tried to get all the peasants onto collective farms that were oriented around historical villages. peasants rebelled by refusing to grow, hiding seed, and slaughtering their own animals before they could be taken from them. groups of state agents went from village to village to literally take grain from peasants.

during this period, WWII also happened. millions of able-bodied men were sent to the front, and the countryside was left to be tended by women and youth. millions of those men never returned to the countryside.

so basically at the end of stalin's reign in 1953, the peasants had been put through hell, squeezed beyond the point of tolerance, depopulated, with no investment, and still expected to produce on lands they didn't own, only to receive a tiny percentage of the harvest that was left after the state took the majority. this tiny amount was meant to act as seed grain for next year, food for their animals, and food for themselves. they were denied internal passports and there was no investment in any kind of village roads or trucks or electrification. they were not paid in cash and no consumer goods were made available to them (even basic things like tools or kerosene for their lamps).

stalin dies in 1953 and khruschev comes in. khruschev used to be a minister in ukraine and was aware of the problems of farmers there. so he was sympathetic, and wanted to make things better (which was at least a step up from "murderous" and "hateful of the peasants"), but everything continued to be extremely huge gambles at extreme urgency, without enough planning or consideration for complex effects. he also believed in lysenkoism (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lysenkoism) and got rid of capable scientists and administrators in favor of lysenko and his followers. and he also loved to reorganize bureaucracy, creating chaos and complexity.

he "opened up" vast areas of kazakhstan for farming (over the objections of local administrators - who he pushed out and replaced with his own people), which was ok for a few years while they exploited the built up natural fertility of the land, but once that was all gone, yields went down and then the environmental consequences started to come in with massive erosion and wind damage.

that's as far as i got so far...i'm only halfway thru the book.

i find myself resorting to nice soviet sayings like "we tried to make it better and it came out the same as always." or a joke my dad told me recently: "what would happen if the USSR took over the sahara desert? in 5 years, there would be a shortage of sand."

as you can see, these sayings help make sense of an extremely complicated set of circumstances that are like...one nightmare piled on another one....

and now you know why so many russian songs are sad!
